solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings)

clue.text: Solver changing euros during travel northwards

definitions.note: 'Solver' is a noun and the answer a pronoun: the setter is talking directly to the person holding the paper, so the word points at the reader rather than swapping into the sentence.

indicators.note: Money changing hands changes into something else, and letters changed do not stay in the order they came in.
During something means in the middle of it, so the changed letters sit inside the other word.

parts.note: to fly somewhere is to travel there — it opens up to hold five more letters

indicators.note: A down entry is written north to south, so wordplay read northwards goes into the grid the other way round.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters, going inside

explanation.surface: A traveller heading north swapping currency along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: Read up the column the entry becomes FLY with the euros jumbled inside it. Guardian setters address the solver often enough that 'solver' and 'you' are worth treating as a standing pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever is working on the clue is the one solving it, and the setter turns round and names the reader as that person.

clue.text: African 10 touring European country

indicators.note: A tour goes round the place it visits, so two letters travel around what sits between them.

parts.note: the figures themselves read as letters: the 1 as an I, the nought as an O
GB is the international plate code for Great Britain

explanation.surface: An African on a tour round a country in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid is full of cross-references, so '10' looks like one and is not: it is the two figures read as letters. GB names Britain rather than a country in the strict sense, which is the clue's one piece of licence.
explanation.definitionFit: The Igbo are one of the largest peoples of southern Nigeria, so a member of them is an African.

clue.text: Couple right to get a stiff drink

parts.note: a brace is a pair — two pheasants, two of anything
R is the standard abbreviation for right, as on a shoebox

explanation.surface: A pair of drinkers claiming their right to something strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' sits at the head of the sentence looking like its subject when it is a word wanting a synonym. The shooting sense, a brace of birds, is the one the setter means.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracer is a drink taken to steady the nerves, and a stiff one is how that drink gets poured.

clue.text: Where treasure is beheld or adornment's seized

indicators.note: Something seized is grabbed and held, and the letters wanted are held unbroken inside the words carrying them.

parts.note: the run starts three letters into the first word and crosses both word breaks without a gap

explanation.surface: Someone catching sight of treasure as the jewellery is snatched.
explanation.walkthrough: A hidden run this long can hide because 'beheld' and 'adornment' are both busy carrying the surface, and the join passes straight through the little word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: El Dorado is the golden city the conquistadors hunted through South America, so the phrase names the place all the treasure was supposed to be.

clue.text: Hands back either Ronnie or Reggie's jacket, escorted off

indicators.note: A jacket is the outside layer, so what is wanted is the letters at the two ends of the name.

parts.note: both names open with the same letter and close with the same letter, so 'either' costs nothing

indicators.note: Milk gone off is not what it was, and letters gone off no longer sit in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: One of a pair of brothers walked off the premises without his coat.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie and Reggie are the Kray twins, the East End gangsters of the 1960s, and the surface trades on them; the wordplay only ever wanted a first letter and a last one.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrocede is to give territory or a right back to whoever held it before, so it is handing the thing back.

clue.text: Superficial motifs featured by ballads

parts.note: to be featured in a film is to be in it
a lay is an old narrative ballad, as in the Lay of the Last Minstrel

explanation.surface: Shallow themes that keep turning up in folk songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superficial' is doing its literal job here, on the surface, rather than its usual insulting one. Lays are the medieval sung poems, a word that survives mainly in Walter Scott and crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Inlays are the patterns set flush into a surface — wood, ivory, mother-of-pearl laid in and polished level — so they are motifs living on the surface.

clue.text: After autumn month, leave Pole in Russian city

indicators.note: Coming after the month means the other two pieces stack up behind it, so the month's letters lead.

parts.note: November falls in autumn, and three letters is how a diary prints it
to go is to leave
a pole and a rod are the same thing, and were once the same unit of length

explanation.surface: Telling a Pole to leave once the autumn month is out.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P pushes the Polish reading hard, and a Russian city with a Pole in it feels plausible enough to chase. It is the piece of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Novgorod is one of the oldest cities in Russia, the medieval trading republic on the road between Moscow and St Petersburg.

clue.text: Called an Uber going across 15 17 in Europe

indicators.note: The letters go across the gaps between the words, running on from one into the next without a break.

parts.note: the run begins on the last letter of the first word and stops one letter short of the end

explanation.surface: Someone ordering a cab to take them over a frontier somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: A brand name barely ten years old is what makes the hiding place work: 'Uber' reads as pure surface. 15 and 17 give the phrase flower border, and the flower is the one that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danube is a river — a flower in the crossword sense, a thing that flows — and it runs along the frontier between several European countries.

clue.text: Pork pie's keeping cool for rest periods

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, and here one word holds another inside itself.

parts.note: pork pies is Cockney rhyming slang for lies, usually shortened to porkies — it opens to take two more letters
what is in is what is fashionable

explanation.surface: A pork pie being kept chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhyming slang is the step to spot: pork pies rhymes with lies, and Londoners shorten it to porkies. 'Cool' is not refrigeration but fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is a morning spent in bed well past the usual hour, so several of them are periods of rest.

clue.text: Trunks stripped off roughly

indicators.note: Clothes stripped off come away from the outside, so the letter at each end goes: the opening T and the closing S.

parts.note: trunks are torsos, the body without its head or limbs

explanation.surface: Swimming trunks peeled off in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the swimwear and the tree are decoys for the anatomical sense of trunks. The enumeration is the tell: two two-letter words cannot be a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Or so' is what gets added to a number when the count is not exact — twenty or so — which is the hedge that 'roughly' makes.

clue.text: One shows relief, like a travelling performer with high camp clothing

indicators.note: Someone high is not in their right state, and these four letters come out of it in a different one.
Clothing goes on the outside, so those letters wrap round the rest.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters, which then split to sit either side
a performer going from town to town is on tour

explanation.surface: A touring entertainer in outrageous stage costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High camp' is a real phrase about theatrical excess, which is exactly why 'high' does not look like an instruction. The relief is the geographer's: how far the land rises.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour map shows relief — the rise and fall of the ground — by drawing lines through all the points at one height.

clue.text: English monarchs drinking one more rum

parts.note: E for English, as a dictionary labels it

indicators.note: What you drink goes down inside you, so the letter being drunk ends up within the monarchs.

parts.note: ER is the royal cypher, Elizabeth Regina, and the plural asks for it twice
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: English kings knocking back another rum.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum the spirit and rum the adjective are the whole joke, and only the second is the definition. ER is the cypher stamped on British postboxes, borrowed here for monarchs in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum in its old adjective sense means odd or strange, so more rum is the comparative of strange.

clue.text: Retailer, one pressing to grab £1,000 after start of week

indicators.note: To grab a thing is to take hold of it, and the word doing the grabbing closes round what it has taken.

parts.note: the one doing the pressing at the ironing board — it splits to take the other letters

indicators.note: The money comes after the day, so its letter follows the day's three rather than leading them.

parts.note: the week starts on Monday, three letters as a diary prints it
a grand is a thousand pounds, G for short

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper snatching a grand at the beginning of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One pressing' sounds like somebody in a hurry and is a person at an ironing board. Ironmongers are the British hardware trade, a word that has outlived most of the shops.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironmonger is the British hardware dealer, selling nails, tools and pans over a counter — a retailer of exactly that stock.

clue.text: Sculptor smuggled cocaine in vehicle heading for Ibiza

indicators.note: A heading sits at the top, so only the first letter of the island is taken.

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle — it opens after its first letter to take what is smuggled
to run guns or drugs is to smuggle them

indicators.note: The drugs go in the vehicle, so those letters sit inside the vehicle's own.

parts.note: C is the standing letter for cocaine
the island's opening letter

explanation.surface: A courier running cocaine out to Ibiza on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug-run surface does all the work: 'smuggled' looks like the instruction to insert and is a word wanting a synonym, while the tiny 'in' is what actually does the inserting.
explanation.definitionFit: Constantin Brancusi was the Romanian modernist of the polished bronze birds and the endless column, and sculpture is what he made.

clue.text: Jersey, say, on female could be violet

indicators.note: In an across entry a piece written on another has been reached after it, so the cattle word follows the single letter.

parts.note: F for female, as on any form
a Jersey is one breed of cow, and a cow lows, which makes it a lower; 'say' flags the example

explanation.surface: Something from Jersey worn by a woman, perhaps in violet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a knitted top in a colour; 'Jersey, say' wants the animal, and a beast that lows is a lower. Together with 17 this entry gives the phrase four other clues point at.
explanation.definitionFit: A violet is one bloom among thousands, so the clue names a single member of the class and 'could be' admits as much.

clue.text: Throwing out spirits, so mixer's drunk without drop of cognac

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and these letters do not stay in theirs.
'Without' in its older sense means outside, so the shuffled letters go round the outside rather than anything being lost.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters; the 's is only the sentence's verb

indicators.note: A drop is the smallest measure of a liquid, and the smallest piece of the word is its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter, the single drop taken from it

explanation.surface: A party where somebody is drunk on mixers and the cognac has run dry.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about drink, and 'spirits' is the pivot the definition swings on. 'Without' meaning outside rather than lacking is the second trap: nothing is deleted here.
explanation.definitionFit: An exorcism is the rite that drives a possessing spirit out of a person or a house, and throwing it out is the whole object of the exercise.

clue.text: Picked up pupil at Eton, perhaps one on edge

indicators.note: What you pick up you hear, so what is wanted is the sound of another word rather than its spelling.

parts.note: Eton is a boarding school, so its pupils live in — 'perhaps' concedes that not every one of them does

explanation.surface: A nervous schoolboy overheard saying something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One on edge' works twice: a jittery person in the surface, a thing lying along an edge in the definition. The two spellings differ by a single letter, which is what makes the sound worth clueing.
explanation.definitionFit: A border is the strip running along the edge of a thing — a country, a garden, a page — so it is named by where it sits.

clue.text: Touching coal, sending off large spark again

parts.note: re means about or concerning — touching the matter of

indicators.note: A player sent off leaves the field, and the letter sent off leaves the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: lignite is brown coal, the soft young kind burnt in power stations
L is the clothing size large, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: Handling coal while a big spark is dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: Knowing that lignite is a coal is the whole clue; losing its L leaves a word that needs no further work. 'Touching' for RE is old legal English — touching the matter of.
explanation.definitionFit: To reignite a fire is to set it going a second time, which is sparking it again.

clue.text: Socialite turns up late, leaving area put in 15 17

indicators.note: A down entry is written from the top, so a word that turns up in it is read the other way round.
What leaves is gone, so the area's letter is missing when the rest is written down.

parts.note: a debutante is the young woman presented at society balls, deb for short — it is then turned
the late are the dead
A is the abbreviation for area, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A socialite turning up late and quitting the district.
explanation.walkthrough: Two short words are taken apart and restacked, and the definition is the garden phrase this puzzle keeps pointing at: 15 17 is a flower border, and plants go into one.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedding plants are the ones set into a border for a season's flowering, so a plant that has been bedded is one put in.

clue.text: 15 17 captured in kind of writing

indicators.note: What is captured is held inside its captor, so the short word sits within the longer one.

parts.note: prose is writing that is not verse — it opens after its first letter
the entry at 17 means an edge, and the three-letter word for an edge is what goes inside

explanation.surface: A garden border being written up on the page.
explanation.walkthrough: Both numbers are cross-references doing different jobs: 15 is the definition, 17 is a piece of the wordplay. Splitting the containing word after its single first letter is the move.
explanation.definitionFit: A primrose is the pale yellow flower of early spring banks and hedgerows, so the entry at 15 covers it as a class covers a member.

clue.text: Rubbish hotel agreed to put up artist

parts.note: rot is rubbish in the sense of nonsense
hotel is H in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: This entry is written downwards, so a word put up in it is read from the bottom back to the top.

parts.note: to say OK is to agree — it is then turned

explanation.surface: A shabby hotel agreeing to take a painter in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish hotel' reads as one insult and is two separate pieces, which is where the clue hides. 'Put up' is doing surface duty too, since a hotel puts guests up.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Rothko painted the huge soft-edged blocks of colour that fill a gallery wall, and painting them was his trade.

clue.text: Playing in the street, almost getting the boot

indicators.note: Almost all of the word is wanted, so it stops one letter short of the end.

parts.note: playing music in the street for coins is busking

explanation.surface: A street musician on the point of being sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the boot' is the idiom the surface sells, being dismissed, while the definition wants the footwear itself. Those boots were the raised ones of Greek tragedy, which makes the performing surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A buskin is the thick-soled boot worn by actors in ancient tragedy, a word kept alive by theatre history and crosswords.

clue.text: Capital city with new basis for all the family

indicators.note: A basis made new is rebuilt, and rebuilding these five letters means setting them in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
a U certificate on a British film means it is passed for viewers of any age

explanation.surface: A city put back up on a new footing that suits everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The U certificate is the British film rating for pictures anyone may watch, and it is the only letter here that 'basis' does not supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Bissau is the port capital of Guinea-Bissau on the West African coast.

clue.text: Ethics done badly leads to atrocities

indicators.note: Done badly, a thing does not come out as it should, and these ten letters do not come out in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Ethical standards handled badly and ending in horrors.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence is true as well as being wordplay, which is what keeps the fodder so quiet: bad ethics really do lead where the definition says.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethnocide is the deliberate destruction of a people's culture, the kind of crime named at war crimes tribunals.

clue.text: Collar turned over by king in 15 17

indicators.note: Turned over means facing the other way, so those three letters are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: to collar a suspect is to nab them — it is then turned
K is the king on a chessboard and in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: An arrest overturned on royal authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 17 reads as a flower border, and the flower is the crossword one: something that flows. That leaves the definition asking for the edge of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower in crossword usage is a thing that flows, a river, and the border of a river is its bank.

clue.text: Extorted money from plot to pocket pounds

indicators.note: What you pocket goes inside, so the money's letter is tucked within the other word.

parts.note: a plot of earth in a garden is a bed — it opens after its first letter
L is the pound of £, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A scheme for trousering somebody else's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' is the garden plot rather than the conspiracy the surface offers, and this grid full of borders and beds is the hint that gardening is in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: To bleed someone is to drain money out of them by steady pressure, and the clue asks for that verb in the past.

clue.text: Heartless shirkers who are going downhill

indicators.note: A heartless word has lost its middle, and the middle of this seven-letter one is a single V.

parts.note: a skiver is British slang for someone dodging work or school

explanation.surface: Work-shy types whose lives are on the slide.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the sentence point the same way — shirkers on the way down — while the definition turns out to be literal and rather cheerful. Skiving is the British word for dodging work.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiers are the people going down the slope on two planks, so the clue names them by what they are doing.

clue.text: Rings about shocking treatment for Geordie and Scouse?

indicators.note: About means round, so the outer word goes round the three letters it is given.

parts.note: to ring someone is to dial them — it opens before its last letter
electroconvulsive therapy, the psychiatric treatment that passes a current through the brain

explanation.surface: Someone ringing round about a brutal course of treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that Tyneside and Liverpool speech are two examples among dozens. ECT is a standing crossword abbreviation for electroconvulsive therapy, and 'shocking' is the pointer to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Geordie is the speech of Tyneside and Scouse that of Liverpool, so the pair of them are two examples of what the answer names.
